chief_complaint: inability to retract prepuce/foreskin over glans penis
hpi_details: A 56-year-old male presents to the clinic with inability to retract the foreskin over the glans penis. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening.
ideas: He thinks he developed an allergic reaction or a stubborn fungal rash from a new laundry detergent or soap.
concerns: He is embarrassed about the problem and worried that he will need a painful adult circumcision that could disrupt intimacy with his wife.
expectations: He hopes to be prescribed a topical steroid cream or soothing ointment today so the skin loosens without needing surgery.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Phimosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Assess for infection, diabetes, lichen sclerosus, and suspicious penile lesions; gentle topical steroid therapy may be appropriate for uncomplicated phimosis, while persistent pathologic phimosis or suspected malignancy warrants urology review.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: inability to retract prepuce/foreskin over glans penis

Key HPI features: A 56-year-old male presents to the clinic with inability to retract the foreskin over the glans penis. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Phimosis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Phimosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Forcing back a tight foreskin, which can cause paraphimosis.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Forcing retraction, missing paraphimosis or urinary retention, or overlooking an ulcerated, bleeding, or indurated penile lesion.
management_principles: Avoid forceful retraction; treat confirmed uncomplicated phimosis with clinician-directed topical steroid and gentle stretching, and refer persistent, scarred, or suspicious cases for urology assessment and possible circumcision.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of inability to retract prepuce/foreskin over glans penis. HPI: phimosis.
reference_soap.objective: Inspect the foreskin and glans for inflammation, scarring, lichen sclerosus, or a suspicious lesion; assess urinary stream and screen for diabetes or recurrent infection as indicated.
reference_soap.assessment: Phimosis; exclude balanitis, lichen sclerosus, paraphimosis, urinary obstruction, and penile malignancy in an adult with new or progressive narrowing.
reference_soap.plan: Avoid forceful retraction. If uncomplicated, consider a time-limited topical steroid with gentle stretching under clinical guidance; arrange urology review for persistent scarring, recurrent infection, suspicious lesions, or consideration of circumcision. Seek emergency care for paraphimosis or inability to pass urine.

red_flags: Paraphimosis with a swollen, painful glans

must_ask.objective: Onset and severity of foreskin tightness
must_ask.say: When did you first notice that your foreskin was difficult to retract, and has it become tighter?
Do you have pain, redness, swelling, itching, or discharge around the head of the penis?
Have you had burning when you urinate, a weak stream, or any difficulty passing urine?
Has the foreskin ever become stuck behind the head of the penis or caused severe swelling?
Do you have diabetes, recurrent genital infections, or a history of skin conditions such as lichen sclerosus?

history.answer: I came in because I haven't been able to pull the foreskin back over the head of my penis.
I first noticed it felt unusually tight about a month ago, and it has gradually become harder and harder to pull back.
It is right at the tip of the penis around the opening of the foreskin.
The foreskin opening has become very narrow and stiff, and right now I cannot pull it back over the head at all.
It has gotten steadily worse over the past few weeks, and it doesn't get any better on its own.
Trying to force it back makes it sting and hurt, but leaving it alone is completely painless.
No, the skin covers the head completely right now and has never gotten stuck behind the head.
I don't have any pain when resting, and there hasn't been any severe swelling or throbbing.
No, I haven't seen any pus, foul-smelling discharge, or bleeding from under the foreskin.
I can still urinate, though the stream seems a bit narrower than usual, but I have never been unable to pee.
Sometimes the foreskin puffs out a little bit like a tiny balloon right as I start to pee, but it empties quickly.
No burning when I pass urine, and I don't feel like I need to run to the bathroom all the time.
No fevers, no chills, and no unexplained weight loss or night sweats.
I had no issues pulling it back until last month, and I have never had foreskin problems in the past.
I haven't seen a doctor for this yet or had any tests done before today.
I tried pulling it back gently in the shower with warm water, but once I felt resistance and pain, I stopped forcing it.
No injuries, no rough friction, and no changes in soaps or body washes.
It makes it very difficult to clean properly, and my wife and I have had to avoid intercourse because stretching it hurts.
No, I don't have any white patches, itchy rashes, or other skin conditions on my body.
No, I haven't noticed excessive thirst, having to drink huge amounts of water, or peeing constantly.
I thought maybe I had an allergic reaction to a new body wash or picked up a fungal rash that made the skin swell up tight.
I feel so embarrassed about this, and I'm really scared you'll tell me I need an operation or circumcision at my age.
I'm hoping you can prescribe a cream or ointment today to help loosen the skin so I won't need any surgery.
I've been generally healthy with no high blood pressure, diabetes, or other chronic conditions.
I have never had any surgeries or stays in the hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink a beer or a glass of wine socially once or twice a month.
I work as an office manager and live at home with my wife.
No one in my family has had penile disorders or urological conditions that I know of.
I have been married for over twenty years in a monogamous relationship, with no history of sexually transmitted infections.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, comfortable, and in no acute distress.
Soft and non-tender, with no suprapubic fullness or palpable urinary bladder distension.
Prepuce is tight and cannot be retracted over the glans penis; a fibrotic constricting ring is visible without purulent discharge, focal ulceration, gross mass, or paraphimotic entrapment.
No inguinal lymphadenopathy or palpable inguinal hernia bilaterally.
No extragenital plaques, hypopigmented atrophic patches, or rash elsewhere on the body.
